explain.say: GE Aviation once made a jet engine fuel nozzle tip from about 20 separate parts brazed together. Now it prints it in one piece from metal powder, about a quarter lighter. That is additive manufacturing: building a part by adding material layer upon layer instead of cutting it away. Look at the steps.

explain.say: Software slices the 3D model into thin layers. Our part is 50 millimetres tall, sliced at 0.2 millimetres, so it needs 250 layers. If each layer takes 30 seconds, the print takes 125 minutes. Thinner layers give a smoother finish but take longer. What happens to print time if you halve the layer height?

explain.say: It roughly doubles! The machine adds each layer in one of seven process families. See the groups? Desktop FDM printers squeeze melted plastic through a nozzle. SLA cures liquid resin with light. Powder bed fusion melts powder with a laser: nylon for prototypes, titanium and nickel alloys for aerospace and medical implants.

Printed parts have quirks. Layers bond less strongly than the material inside a layer, so an FDM part is often weakest when pulled along the build direction. This is anisotropy. Overhangs need supports, and metal parts often need heat treatment to relieve stress. How should you orient a printed hook?

draw.text: Anisotropy: strength depends on direction; weakest across layers

explain.say: So the load runs along the layers, not across them! Fantastic. When should you print? See the comparison: print complex, light or one-off parts; machine simple parts in volume. Exam tip: design for additive by merging parts and using lattices, not just by copying a machined design.

faq.a: A 3D model is sliced into thin layers, and a machine builds the part one layer at a time by melting, curing or binding material where the slice says, until the full shape is complete.

faq.q: How does layer height affect a print?
faq.a: Thinner layers give smoother surfaces and finer detail but need more layers, so print time rises roughly in proportion. A 50 millimetre part at 0.2 millimetre layers needs 250 layers.

faq.q: What are the main types of additive manufacturing?
faq.a: The standard groups seven families: material extrusion, vat photopolymerisation, powder bed fusion, material jetting, binder jetting, directed energy deposition and sheet lamination.

faq.q: Why are 3D printed parts weaker in one direction?
faq.a: The bond between layers is weaker than the material within each layer, so parts are usually weakest when loaded across the layers. This is called anisotropy.

faq.q: When should I use 3D printing instead of machining?
faq.a: Choose printing for complex shapes, internal channels, lattices, part consolidation and small numbers. Choose machining for simple shapes, tight tolerances, full material strength and larger volumes.

facts: ISO/ASTM 52900 groups additive manufacturing into seven process categories.
GE's printed LEAP fuel nozzle tip replaced about 20 parts with one and is about 25 % lighter.
